main_skill: Manage multiple patients with very limited resources under ethical pressure
core_question: Who needs attention first, and how can I manage everyone with very limited resources?

protocol_reference.usage_note: Underlying triage categories carry over from mass-casualty logic.

protocol_reference.attribution: CDC MMWR Guidelines for Field Triage of Injured Patients

protocol_reference.usage_note: Resource-need-based acuity for the lower-severity patients in this level.

protocol_reference.attribution: 1000-Word Philosophy and PMC (four principles of biomedical ethics)
protocol_reference.usage_note: The two scarce-resource allocation decisions (VENTILATOR_ALLOCATION and OR_ALLOCATION) are explicitly tagged against the four principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. The optimal option in each case applies justice/utility (allocate the scarce resource to maximize salvageable lives) balanced with beneficence and non-maleficence, consistent with standard crisis-standards-of-care ethics used in disaster medicine.

note: All names, vitals, and clinical details below are entirely fictional training content generated for simulation purposes. This scenario depicts a fictional building-fire mass-casualty incident with severely constrained hospital resources, for emergency-ethics and triage training only.
scope_note: As with Level 4, each patient carries one condensed management decision rather than a 4-step tree, to keep the level playable under the intended time pressure. The two resource-allocation decisions (ventilator, OR/surgeon) are the level's centerpiece and are fully branched with explicit ethical-principle tagging.

dialogue: Doctor, we have a second wave from the apartment fire -- six more patients, and we're already stretched thin.
We have exactly one ventilator, one operating room with one surgeon, two units of blood, one spare oxygen cylinder, and one ICU bed left for the rest of the shift.
Some of these decisions won't have a clean answer. I need you to make the call.

patients.name: Kabir Anand
patients.chief_complaint: Severe smoke inhalation, singed airway, in reversible respiratory failure

medical_report.name: Kabir Anand
medical_report.past_medical_history: Nil significant, previously fit and well
medical_report.injury_summary: Severe smoke inhalation with singed nasal hair and soot in airway, hypoxic respiratory failure, otherwise structurally healthy lungs and heart -- high likelihood of full recovery if ventilated promptly
medical_report.prognosis_with_ventilation: Good - reversible injury, expected to wean within days
medical_report.prognosis_without_ventilation: Poor - likely progression to respiratory arrest within the hour

patients.name: Meenu Bhatt
patients.chief_complaint: Severe smoke inhalation with extensive full-thickness burns to chest and airway

medical_report.name: Meenu Bhatt
medical_report.past_medical_history: Longstanding severe lung disease (details unknown, family not yet contactable)
medical_report.injury_summary: Severe smoke inhalation with extensive full-thickness burns to chest wall and airway, combined with pre-existing severe chronic lung disease
medical_report.prognosis_with_ventilation: Guarded to poor - extensive airway burns and underlying lung disease make successful weaning unlikely

patients.name: Arjun Verma
patients.chief_complaint: Fell during evacuation, active intra-abdominal hemorrhage from a ruptured spleen

medical_report.name: Arjun Verma
medical_report.injury_summary: Active intra-abdominal hemorrhage, hemodynamically unstable and worsening by the minute without surgical source control
medical_report.prognosis_with_surgery: Good if operated on within the next 20-30 minutes
medical_report.prognosis_without_surgery: Very poor - expected to progress to hemorrhagic shock and arrest

patients.name: Farida Sheikh
patients.chief_complaint: Open femur fracture with vascular injury to the leg during the evacuation

medical_report.name: Farida Sheikh
medical_report.injury_summary: Open femur fracture with a vascular injury; a temporary tourniquet is currently controlling hemorrhage but the limb is at risk without definitive surgical repair
medical_report.prognosis_with_surgery: Good, including a good chance of limb salvage if operated on within a few hours
medical_report.prognosis_without_surgery: Life is not immediately threatened with the tourniquet in place, but limb viability declines the longer surgery is delayed

patients.name: Nikhil Bose
patients.chief_complaint: Mild smoke inhalation, walking and talking normally

medical_report.name: Nikhil Bose
medical_report.injury_summary: Mild smoke inhalation, mild cough, no respiratory distress

patients.name: Ritu Malhotra
patients.chief_complaint: Deep laceration to the thigh with ongoing moderate hemorrhage

medical_report.name: Ritu Malhotra
medical_report.injury_summary: Deep thigh laceration with moderate ongoing blood loss, responsive to direct pressure but likely to need transfusion

nurse_dialogue: Doctor, both Kabir and Meenu need the ventilator right now, and we only have one.

Kabir's lungs and airway are otherwise healthy -- his odds are good if we ventilate him. Meenu has extensive airway burns and longstanding lung disease -- even with the ventilator, her chances are much lower.
There's no easy answer here. What do you want to do?

options.text: Give the ventilator to Kabir, whose reversible injury gives him a substantially higher likelihood of survival. Support Meenu with the highest level of non-invasive oxygen and comfort care available, and reassess immediately if the ventilator frees up.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Justice (utility) balanced with beneficence and non-maleficence -- allocating a scarce, life-sustaining resource to maximize the number of lives saved is the standard crisis-standards-of-care approach when one resource cannot serve two patients equally well
nurse_response: Understood, Doctor. Kabir's oxygenating well now. I'll stay close to Meenu and keep her as comfortable as possible.

options.text: Give the ventilator to Meenu because she arrived first and it would be unfair to prioritize a younger patient by that reasoning alone.
options.ethics_principle_applied: A narrow reading of justice-as-first-come-first-served, applied without weighing likely benefit -- ethically defensible as a tiebreaker between similar prognoses, but not appropriate here given the large prognostic gap
nurse_response: Doctor, Kabir's crashing -- he needed that ventilator far more than she did.

options.text: Give the ventilator to Kabir because he is younger and 'more deserving' of the resource.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Misapplies justice as a crude social-worth judgment (age/perceived deservingness) rather than a clinical likelihood-of-benefit assessment -- even though the outcome happens to match option A, the reasoning itself is an ethical error the simulation should flag
nurse_response: The outcome may be the same, Doctor, but we should be clear it's about his likelihood of recovery -- not his age.

options.text: Attempt to alternate the single ventilator back and forth between both patients every few minutes.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Violates non-maleficence -- splitting inadequate, intermittent ventilatory support between two critically hypoxic patients risks harming both rather than adequately treating either
nurse_response: Doctor, neither of them is getting enough support this way -- they're both declining.

nurse_dialogue: Doctor, Arjun and Farida both need the OR and our one surgeon.
Arjun is actively bleeding internally and getting worse by the minute. Farida's bleeding is controlled with a tourniquet for now, but her leg is at risk the longer we wait.
We can only operate on one of them right now. What do you want to do?

options.text: Take Arjun to the OR first, since his bleeding is uncontrolled and immediately life-threatening. Maintain Farida's tourniquet, reassess limb viability continuously, and take her to the OR the moment the surgeon is free.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Justice/utility applied through immediacy of threat to life over threat to limb, consistent with non-maleficence (avoiding the greater harm of preventable death) while still actively working to preserve Farida's limb

vitals_delta_P4.note: Limb ischemia time is accruing but life is not in immediate danger

nurse_response: Understood, Doctor. Arjun's in theatre now. I'm watching Farida's leg closely and the surgeon will move to her the moment he's free.

options.text: Take Farida to the OR first because limb loss is a devastating outcome and should be avoided at all costs.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Prioritizes a limb-threatening injury over an immediately life-threatening hemorrhage -- a well-intentioned but ethically and clinically inverted application of non-maleficence, since preventable death outweighs limb loss in triage priority
nurse_response: Doctor, Arjun didn't make it to the OR in time -- his bleeding couldn't wait.

options.text: Let the two patients or their families decide between themselves who goes first.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Over-extends respect for autonomy into a decision that requires clinical judgment the patients and families cannot safely make under this time pressure -- autonomy matters, but not as a substitute for triage responsibility in an immediately life-threatening scenario
nurse_response: Doctor, we lost precious minutes to that conversation -- Arjun needs the OR right now.

options.text: Delay both and wait to see if either patient's condition resolves on its own.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Violates non-maleficence for both patients -- inaction while a definitive resource is available is itself a harmful choice

vitals_delta_P4.BP_mmHg: stable but limb ischemia time increasing

nurse_response: Doctor, Arjun has arrested -- we needed to act.

nurse_dialogue: Meenu is on maximal non-invasive support, Doctor. Her family has just arrived. What would you like to do?

options.text: Speak honestly with the family about her prognosis, continue maximal comfort-focused support, and reassess for the ventilator immediately if it becomes free.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Autonomy (honest information for the family/surrogate decision-makers) combined with continued beneficence and non-maleficence
nurse_response: The family appreciated the honesty, Doctor. We're keeping her as comfortable as possible.

options.text: Avoid the family and give no updates.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Violates respect for autonomy and the family's right to information
nurse_response: Doctor, the family is distressed and has no idea what's happening -- they deserve an update.

options.text: Promise the family the ventilator will definitely become available for her soon.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Violates honesty within autonomy -- making a promise about scarce-resource availability that cannot be guaranteed
nurse_response: Doctor, we shouldn't have promised that -- it isn't something we can guarantee.

options.text: Withdraw all support immediately without discussion, assuming the outcome is inevitable.
options.ethics_principle_applied: Violates non-maleficence and autonomy -- withdrawing support without reassessment or family communication
nurse_response: Doctor, that wasn't the right call without reassessing her first and talking to the family.

nurse_dialogue: Farida's tourniquet is holding, Doctor, and the surgeon is finishing with Arjun. What would you like to do while we wait?

options.text: Continuously reassess limb perfusion, keep her comfortable with analgesia, and take her to the OR the moment the surgeon is free.
nurse_response: Good, Doctor. The surgeon is ready for her now -- limb still viable.

options.text: Leave the tourniquet in place indefinitely without reassessment.
nurse_response: Doctor, the delay has put the limb at higher risk than it needed to be.

options.text: Loosen the tourniquet periodically to 'let blood flow' without surgical control available.
nurse_response: Doctor, loosening it caused rebleeding without surgical control ready -- that put her at serious risk.

options.text: Give her no analgesia while she waits, to 'save resources'.
nurse_response: Doctor, she's in unnecessary pain -- analgesia was available and appropriate here.

nurse_dialogue: Nikhil's stable and walking, Doctor -- mild smoke inhalation. What would you like to do?

options.text: Give supportive care (observation, mild oxygen if needed), and discharge with safety-netting advice once clear.
nurse_response: He's doing well, Doctor -- clear for discharge with advice to return if breathing worsens.

options.text: Use the level's one remaining spare oxygen cylinder on him even though his saturation is normal.
nurse_response: He's fine, Doctor, but that was our last spare cylinder -- now unavailable if Kabir or Meenu need backup.

options.text: Ignore him completely given the other critical patients.
nurse_response: Doctor, he's fine, but a quick check and reassurance would have been appropriate.

options.text: Admit him to the single remaining ICU bed 'to be cautious'.
nurse_response: Doctor, that used our only ICU bed on a patient who didn't need it.

nurse_dialogue: Ritu's thigh wound is still oozing, Doctor, and she's tachycardic. We have two units of blood left. What would you like to do?

options.text: Apply firm direct pressure, secure IV access, transfuse one unit of blood while monitoring response, and reserve the second unit in case another patient needs it.
nurse_response: She's responding well, Doctor, and we've still got one unit of blood in reserve.

options.text: Transfuse both remaining units of blood into her immediately, even though one is responding well to the first.
nurse_response: She's stable, Doctor, but we now have zero blood units left for anyone else tonight.

options.text: Apply pressure only and withhold transfusion despite ongoing blood loss and rising heart rate.
nurse_response: Doctor, she's getting worse -- she needed that transfusion.

options.text: Wait for lab cross-match confirmation before applying any pressure to the wound.
nurse_response: Doctor, we shouldn't have delayed pressure on an actively bleeding wound.

nurse_dialogue: Kabir's ventilated and stable, Doctor. What's the plan for ongoing monitoring?

options.text: Continue ventilatory support with regular reassessment and plan for the single ICU bed once available.
nurse_response: He's holding steady, Doctor, and first in line for the ICU bed.

options.text: Disconnect him from the ventilator early since he 'looks better'.
nurse_response: Doctor, he decompensated when support was withdrawn too early.

options.text: Leave him on the ventilator with no further monitoring plan.
nurse_response: He's stable for now, Doctor, but we need an actual ongoing plan.

options.text: Give the ICU bed to someone else without a clear reassessment of Kabir's needs.
nurse_response: Doctor, he needed that bed -- let's revisit this decision.

flow_control.explanation: No decision node's option points directly at another patient's decision node. The engine advances between patients/nodes ONLY by following the fixed sequence below, never by an embedded next_decision cross-reference.

sequence.node: implicit in OR_ALLOCATION outcome, no further P3 node in this level

endings.level_outcome_logic: Level 5 result is computed across all 6 patients and both allocation decisions. SUCCESS requires: (1) the higher-survivability patient received the scarce resource in both VENTILATOR_ALLOCATION and OR_ALLOCATION, (2) no patient reaches CRITICAL_ENDPOINT, and (3) all six patients reach a STABILIZED, STABLE_*, or an appropriately-managed comfort-care status. The ethics_reasoning_quality score is tracked separately from the raw outcome, since some options (e.g. VENTILATOR_ALLOCATION option C) can produce the correct clinical outcome via flawed ethical reasoning, which the performance report flags for review.

SUCCESS_WITH_PENALTY.banner: CRITICAL OVERLOAD MANAGED (RESOURCE-INEFFICIENT / ETHICAL REASONING FLAGGED)

FAILURE.banner: CRITICAL OVERLOAD - PREVENTABLE LOSS OF LIFE
